entries.topic: Primaries, turnout, safe seats and the two-party system

claims.text: Ballotpedia (Aug 2026): Republican Party primaries are closed in 23 states, open in 14, semi-closed in 10; Democratic primaries closed in 17, open in 18, semi-closed in 12; top-two or top-four variants in 5 states. Closed: voter must be affiliated with the party; semi-closed: unaffiliated voters may choose a party primary

BPC: turnout of all eligible voters in 2022 primaries was 21.3%, up on the previous four cycles; states with more open systems averaged 24.5%, semi-open 21.5%, closed 20.7%; top-two/top-four about 3 points higher

Unite America (advocacy, 8 Oct 2024): 87% of House races (380 seats) 'effectively decided' by 7% of eligible voters (18.1M) in 2024 primaries; 169 members ran unopposed in the primary for a safe seat; method and definition of 'decided' not given on the page
Cook 2025 PVI: 87 districts between D+5 and R+5, 56 (about 64%) held by Democrats; median seat Republican-tilted
Cook (2023): 82 of 435 districts between R+5 and D+5, down 50% from 164 in 1999; 58% of the decline since 1997 from areas trending redder or bluer (realignment/sorting) rather than redistricting
Cook 2026 PVI: ten states redrew for 2026; median House seat R+3, two points redder than before; map 'more skewed towards Republicans and less elastic'

Bloomberg Government/Political Wire 3 May 2026: Cook listed 16 toss-up House seats (before Florida's new map), 16 more leaning; outcome all but predetermined in more than 400 seats; possibly the fewest competitive seats since 1984

Duverger's law: single-member plurality districts tend to produce two dominant parties via a mechanical effect (thinly spread small parties win few seats) and a psychological effect (voters avoid 'wasting' votes); Perot won 19% in 1992 and no electoral votes; Duverger saw it as a tendency, not absolute

Ballotpedia (July 2026): 48 states have some form of sore loser law barring a candidate who lost a party primary from running as independent or another party's nominee for the same office; Connecticut and New York have none

Pew (survey 17-30 Nov 2025, n=10,357; published 15 Jan 2026): 37% say 'I often wish there were more political parties to choose from' describes them extremely/very well; Democrats/leaners 46%, Republicans/leaners 29%; ages 18-49 44%, 65+ 25%

entries.topic: Gerrymandering: Rucho, Moore v. Harper and the 2025-26 mid-decade redistricting war

claims.text: 1812: Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry signed a redistricting bill creating a contorted state senate district favouring his Democratic-Republicans over the Federalists; a Boston Gazette cartoon of 26 March 1812 drew it as a winged monster and the label blended Gerry with 'salamander'

Rucho v. Common Cause, 27 June 2019, 5-4 (Roberts; Kagan dissenting with Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor): partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions beyond federal courts, which are 'not equipped to apportion political power as a matter of fairness'; districting assigned to legislatures 'expressly checked and balanced by the Federal Congress'; Kagan: gerrymanders 'debased and dishonored our democracy'; North Carolina's 2016 map drawn by Republicans to subordinate non-Republican voters (district court)

Companion case Lamone v. Benisek (27 June 2019): Maryland's 2011 map drawn by Democratic-led state government; 6th district redrawn, registered Republicans fell by about 70,000; Republican Roscoe Bartlett lost in 2012 to John Delaney by more than 20 points; Court vacated and remanded

Moore v. Harper, 27 June 2023, 6-3: Court rejected the independent state legislature theory; state legislatures remain bound by state constitutions including state-court judicial review of federal election rules; arose from North Carolina Republicans' map struck by the state supreme court

Ballotpedia (28 Sept 2026): new 2026 maps in effect: Texas +5R (legislature, 29 Aug 2025; SCOTUS allowed 4 Dec 2025), California Prop 50 +5D (voters 4 Nov 2025), North Carolina +1R (22 Oct 2025), Ohio +2R (commission, 31 Oct 2025), Utah +1D (court-chosen map, 10 Nov 2025), Florida +4R (4 May 2026), Tennessee +1R (7 May 2026), Louisiana +1R (29 May 2026), Alabama +1R (2 June 2026); projected net +9R across nine maps

Ballotpedia (28 Sept 2026): Missouri's map (28 Sept 2025, +1R) blocked for 2026 pending a veto referendum, 2022 map in use; Virginia's map (signed 21 Feb 2026, aiming at 10D-1R after voters approved an amendment 21 Apr 2026) blocked by the state supreme court 8 May 2026, SCOTUS denied stay 15 May; Indiana's Senate rejected a map on 11 Dec 2025

Louisiana v. Callais, 29 April 2026: Supreme Court held Louisiana's map with a second majority-Black district an unconstitutional racial gerrymander; Louisiana redrew and other states including Tennessee followed
